chapters.title: Community-Acquired Pneumonia
chapters.objective: Recognise CAP at the bedside, stratify severity with CURB-65 / PSI, and pick the right empiric antibiotic for outpatient, ward, and ICU settings.

blocks.text: Recognise CAP at the bedside, stratify severity with CURB-65 / PSI, and pick the right empiric antibiotic for outpatient, ward, and ICU settings.

blocks.html: Community-acquired pneumonia (CAP) is an acute infection of the lung parenchyma that arises outside a hospital or long-term care facility and presents within 48 hours of admission. It is one of the highest-yield Step 2 CK topics — it appears across Internal Medicine, Pediatrics, and Emergency Medicine blocks, and the question stem almost always turns on a single decision: where do you treat this patient?

items: Incidence: ~5–6 cases per 1,000 adults/year in the US; >1 million annual hospitalisations.
Most common typical pathogen: Streptococcus pneumoniae.
Severity score: CURB-65 — 0–1 outpatient, 2 admit ward, ≥3 consider ICU.
Empiric inpatient antibiotic: beta-lactam (ceftriaxone) + macrolide (azithromycin) — covers typical AND atypical.
Diagnosis confirmed by CXR showing infiltrate; do NOT defer antibiotics waiting for imaging in unstable patients.

blocks.html: CAP causes more than a million hospital admissions per year in the United States and remains the leading infectious cause of death in adults. Mortality is bimodal: very low in healthy outpatients (<1%) and substantial in ICU patients (15–30%). The highest-risk groups are children under 2 and adults over 65, both because of immune-system architecture (immature in young, senescent in old) and because comorbidities concentrate at the age extremes.

items: Smoking — impairs mucociliary clearance
COPD / asthma — structurally damaged airways colonise more easily
Immunosuppression — chemotherapy, HIV, transplant, chronic steroids
Recent viral URI — disrupts respiratory epithelium and predisposes to bacterial superinfection
Aspiration risk — stroke, dementia, alcoholism, poor dentition

blocks.text: Etiology — typical vs atypical vs viral

blocks.html: Pathogen family shapes the empiric antibiotic choice more than any individual species. The board exam tests whether you can recognise patterns: lobar consolidation with rusty sputum → pneumococcus; subacute dry cough + headache in a college student → Mycoplasma; recent travel + diarrhea + hyponatremia → Legionella; post-influenza staphylococcal superinfection with cavitation → MRSA.

rows: S. pneumoniae · H. influenzae · Moraxella catarrhalis
Lobar consolidation, productive cough, high fever, rusty sputum (pneumococcus)
Subacute, dry cough, headache, extrapulmonary symptoms; Legionella adds diarrhea + ↓Na⁺
Diffuse interstitial pattern; often precedes secondary bacterial superinfection
Cavitating necrotising pneumonia after flu illness
Right lower lobe (upright) or right upper/lower lobe (supine); foul-smelling sputum; lung abscess

blocks.text: "SHAFT" for typical pneumonia bugs you can't miss: Streptococcus pneumoniae · Haemophilus influenzae · Atypicals (Mycoplasma/Chlamydophila/Legionella) · Flu (and post-flu Staph) · Tuberculosis (always consider in chronic cough, weight loss, night sweats).

blocks.html: Inhaled organisms reach the alveoli, evade ciliary clearance and alveolar macrophages, and trigger an inflammatory cascade. Alveoli fill with neutrophil-rich exudate (consolidation), which impairs gas exchange via V/Q mismatch — alveoli are perfused but not ventilated. The result is hypoxemia despite normal-or-elevated minute ventilation. Systemic cytokine release drives fever, leukocytosis, and (in severe cases) sepsis.

Classic typical-CAP presents acutely: high fever (>38.5°C), productive cough with purulent or rusty sputum, pleuritic chest pain, and dyspnea. On exam: tachypnea, tachycardia, and focal findings over the consolidated lobe — crackles, egophony (E→A change), increased tactile fremitus, and dullness to percussion. Atypical pneumonia is subacute (days to a week of malaise + dry cough + headache) with relatively benign lung exam — the so-called "walking pneumonia."

blocks.text: Any one of these is a red flag that pushes you toward admission, regardless of the rest of the picture: RR ≥30, SBP <90, SpO₂ <90% on room air, altered mental status, multilobar infiltrate, or BUN >19 mg/dL.

blocks.html: Chest X-ray is the diagnostic anchor and should not be skipped — the question stem will tell you about an infiltrate, lobar or interstitial, that confirms the diagnosis. For admitted patients add CBC (leukocytosis with left shift), basic metabolic panel, blood cultures × 2 before antibiotics, sputum gram stain + culture, and urinary antigens for Pneumococcus and Legionella. Procalcitonin can support bacterial etiology but is not used to withhold antibiotics in a clinically convincing case.

items: Step 1. Focused history (fever, cough character, duration, sick contacts, recent travel, smoking, comorbidities).
Step 2. Vital signs + auscultation. Calculate respiratory rate and oxygen saturation explicitly.
Step 3. Order chest X-ray — PA + lateral if stable, portable if not.
Step 4. Labs: CBC, BMP. Add blood cultures + sputum + urinary antigens if admitting.
Step 5. Compute CURB-65 (or full PSI) and decide disposition before writing the antibiotic order.

rows: Often subtle in elderly — ask family
Count it for a full 30 seconds yourself; staff tend to round to 18-20
Single biggest risk factor for mortality

blocks.text: CURB-65 → disposition: 0–1 = Outpatient · 2 = Ward · 3+ = consider ICU. Score 2 with comorbidity (COPD, CHF, CKD) → err on admission.

rows: Low-grade fever, normal/clear CXR, hypoxia disproportionate to exam, risk factors (immobility, OCPs, malignancy). D-dimer / CTPA if suspicious.
Bilateral findings, orthopnea, JVD, S₃ gallop, elevated BNP/NT-proBNP. Cardiomegaly + Kerley B lines on CXR.
Wheezing, prolonged expiratory phase, minimal/no infiltrate. Known underlying disease.
Cough but no infiltrate on CXR. Mostly viral. Antibiotics not routinely indicated.
Smoker, weight loss, hemoptysis, recurrent post-obstructive pneumonia in the same location.
Chronic cough, night sweats, weight loss, exposure history, upper-lobe cavitary infiltrate.

blocks.html: Empiric coverage is the actual exam question. Memorise the four buckets. Always cover atypicals in the inpatient setting because Legionella mortality is high and the clinical picture overlaps.

rows: Outpatient with comorbidity (COPD, CHF, CKD, DM, immunosuppression)
If MRSA risk: add vancomycin or linezolid. If Pseudomonas risk: replace ceftriaxone with piperacillin/tazobactam or cefepime.

blocks.text: MRSA risk factors = recent hospitalisation, IV drug use, post-influenza necrotising pneumonia, known colonisation. Pseudomonas risk factors = structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, severe COPD), recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, chronic steroid use. If neither, you do NOT need vancomycin + zosyn for routine inpatient CAP.

items: Parapneumonic effusion → empyema — adjacent pleural fluid; if infected (empyema) requires thoracentesis + chest tube drainage in addition to antibiotics.
Lung abscess — cavity with air-fluid level; favoured by aspiration and anaerobic infection; extend coverage to anaerobes (clindamycin, amoxicillin-sulbactam).
Sepsis / septic shock — the most common cause of CAP mortality. Recognise early via qSOFA ≥ 2; treat per Surviving Sepsis bundle (cultures, antibiotics within 1 hour, fluids).
ARDS — bilateral infiltrates, PaO₂/FiO₂ < 300, requires mechanical ventilation with lung-protective settings (6 mL/kg ideal body weight, plateau pressure ≤ 30).

blocks.html: Outpatient mortality is under 1%. In-hospital mortality on the ward runs 5–10%; ICU mortality 15–30%, climbing higher with shock or ARDS. Time to first appropriate antibiotic is the single biggest modifiable mortality factor — every hour of delay in septic patients carries measurable additional risk. Most patients improve clinically within 48–72 hours of starting effective therapy; cough can persist for 4 weeks and fatigue often longer. Reinfection risk is mildly elevated for 12 months.

blocks.vignette:
A 68-year-old man with a 30 pack-year smoking history and COPD on tiotropium presents to the ED with 3 days of productive cough, fever to 38.9°C, and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. He has had two days of malaise and decreased appetite. He denies recent travel, sick contacts, or aspiration events.

Vital signs: T 38.9°C, HR 110, RR 28, BP 102/64, SpO₂ 92% on room air.

Exam: Alert and fully oriented. Crackles, egophony, and dullness to percussion in the right lower lung field. No JVD, no peripheral edema.

Labs: WBC 16,400 with 84% neutrophils, BUN 22 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1, Na 136, lactate 1.8.

Imaging: Chest X-ray shows right lower lobe consolidation. No effusion. No cavitation.

Question: Which is the most appropriate next step?

quiz.qstem: Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Discharge home on amoxicillin 1 g PO TID with 48-hour follow-up.
Admit to the medical ward and start IV ceftriaxone + azithromycin.
Admit to the ICU and start broad-spectrum coverage including vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam.
Order CT pulmonary angiography to rule out pulmonary embolism before any antibiotics.
Discharge home on levofloxacin 750 mg PO daily with 48-hour follow-up.

feedback.headline: Correct: B — Admit to ward + IV ceftriaxone + azithromycin
feedback.body: Compute CURB-65 explicitly: Confusion 0 (alert) · Urea 1 (BUN 22 > 19) · RR 0 (28 < 30) · BP 0 (SBP > 90, DBP > 60) · 65 1 (age 68). Total = 2. CURB-65 of 2 supports admission. Combine with the COPD comorbidity and you have an inpatient non-ICU patient. Standard empiric coverage is beta-lactam + macrolide (ceftriaxone + azithromycin) — covers typical pneumococcus/H. flu AND atypicals. A and E are wrong on disposition (CURB-65 = 2 means admit, not outpatient) regardless of drug choice. C over-treats — there are no MRSA or Pseudomonas risk factors, no shock, no ICU-level severity. D chases an unlikely PE; the clinical picture (productive cough + fever + leukocytosis + lobar consolidation) is classic CAP and antibiotics should not be delayed.

cards.front: Atypical CAP pathogens — three to remember
cards.back: Mycoplasma · Chlamydophila · Legionella. Inpatient regimens MUST cover atypicals (Legionella mortality is high).
Recent hospitalisation, IV drug use, post-influenza necrotising pneumonia, known MRSA colonisation. Add vancomycin or linezolid.
Structural lung disease (bronchiectasis, severe COPD), recent broad-spectrum antibiotics, chronic steroid use. Replace ceftriaxone with piperacillin/tazobactam or cefepime.

cards.front: Single biggest modifiable mortality factor in severe CAP
cards.back: Time to first appropriate antibiotic. Within 1 hour for septic patients (Surviving Sepsis bundle).

cards.front: Pleural effusion in CAP — when to drain
cards.back: Empyema (infected fluid) OR effusion >10 mm on lateral decubitus film with positive Gram stain / pH <7.2 / glucose <40. Thoracentesis + chest tube.
